presentingComplaint: Dry cough, low-grade fever and headache for 6 days, now with mild breathlessness
history: A 24-year-old previously healthy university student presents with a 6-day history of low-grade fever, malaise, sore throat and headache, followed by a persistent dry, hacking cough over the last 3-4 days. She reports mild retrosternal chest discomfort with coughing and some breathlessness on exertion. No rigors, no purulent sputum, no hemoptysis. A roommate had a similar prolonged cough illness 2 weeks ago. No significant travel, no comorbidities, non-smoker, no sick contacts with TB, no recent hospitalization or antibiotic use.
examination: Alert, mildly unwell but not toxic-appearing. Oropharynx mildly injected without exudate. Chest: scattered crepitations at the left lower zone, no dullness to percussion, no wheeze. No skin rash. Cardiovascular and abdominal exam unremarkable.
imaging: Chest X-ray: patchy reticulonodular/interstitial infiltrate in the left lower lobe, disproportionately mild compared to clinical findings, no effusion or cavitation
microbiology: Sputum Gram stain: no organisms seen, mixed flora
finalDiagnosis: Community-acquired pneumonia, atypical presentation (Mycoplasma pneumoniae), non-severe (CURB-65 = 0)
stewardship: Outpatient empirical therapy targeting atypical organisms: a macrolide (e.g., azithromycin) or doxycycline as first-line per IDSA/ATS 2019 for a healthy young adult without comorbidities; a respiratory fluoroquinolone reserved as alternative if macrolide resistance or intolerance/allergy.
contraindications: Avoid fluoroquinolone as first-line in an otherwise healthy young adult without comorbidities (reserve for treatment failure/allergy)
edgeCases: Chest X-ray findings are often subtly disproportionate to clinical exam ("walking pneumonia") in Mycoplasma, which can lead to under-triage or misdiagnosis as bronchitis
Cold agglutinin-associated hemolysis is a recognized extrapulmonary complication and should prompt hemoglobin/haptoglobin monitoring if anemia or jaundice develops
Mycoplasma serology (IgM) can be falsely negative early in illness or falsely positive from past infection; PCR is more specific where available
Household/close-contact clustering (roommate with similar illness) supports atypical/community outbreak pathogens over typical bacterial pneumonia
expectedMaiK: Young, non-toxic patient with a subacute prodrome, dry cough, and CXR-exam dissociation strongly suggests atypical CAP (Mycoplasma); CURB-65 is 0, so outpatient macrolide/doxycycline therapy is appropriate without need for hospitalization.
